->### CAPITOLO XVI.<-

->*Delli retrosi fatti per la percussione dell' acqua negli obbietti dell' argine.*<-

Sempre infra l' onda colonnale, e l' argine dove tale onda è cres
si generano retrosi. Provasi, perchè cade l' acque dal colmo dell' onda colonnale, verso l' accrescimento della corrente, ma dalla potenza di essa corrente viene sospinta, e tirata al comun corso dell' acqua; cade medesimamente l' acqua dal colmo dell' onda verso l' argine (fig. 69. tav. 13), ma quivi perchè la corrente resta impedita e ritardata dal moto trasversale della medesima onda, con maggiore impeto penetrandola discende verso l' argine, e percotendola fa un retroso.

->### CAPITOLO XVII.<-

->*Del medesimo.*<-

In ogni percussione d' acqua nell' argine ristretta, e nell' obbietto dell' argine si generano retrosi dalla superficie al fondo. Perchè l' acqua nella percussione s' alza per la linea dell' altezza dell' argine, o dell' obbietto, ed acquistando peso discende al piede, dove nel mezzo del discenso incontrando quella parte dell' acqua, che prima si voltò al fondo, viene risospinta alla superficie, e quivi da nuov' acqua sopraggiunta, cacciata al fondo con vari raccoglimenti viene portata dietro al corso dell' acqua.

->### CAPITOLO XVIII.<-

->*Del medesimo.*<-

L' argine, che fia tirato indietro per dare maggiore larghezza al canale, fia causa di generare subito retroso. Provasi, perchè il fiume che acquista subita larghezza, acquista ancora subita larghezza d' acqua, e l' acqua che s' allarga ancora si viene ad abbassare di profondità;

<meta>This page continues the discussion of fluid dynamics, specifically how the "power" (momentum) and "weight" (gravity) of water interact when two flows meet or when water hits an obstacle. It transitions from the interaction of two currents to the interaction between a current and the river bank.</meta>

LEONARDO DA VINCI 346

whereby, through the weight it has gained, it increases in power and strikes with force against the water that previously overcame it, so that the line of the eddies <term>retrosi</term> <note>circular or backward-flowing water patterns, such as whirlpools or eddies</note> bends in the opposite direction; where it was previously convex, it becomes concave. In this way, the smaller body of water is often pushed by the larger, and the larger is pushed by the smaller when the latter possesses less power <term>potenza</term> <note>the force, momentum, or kinetic energy of a current</note>.

->### CHAPTER XVI.<-

->*On the eddies formed by the impact of water against obstacles along the bank.*<-

Eddies are always generated between the columnar wave <term>onda colonnale</term> <note>a wave that rises in a column-like shape, often where currents meet or hit an obstacle</note> and the bank where such a wave has grown. This is proven because the water falls from the crest of the columnar wave toward the acceleration of the current, but it is pushed and pulled into the general flow of the water by the power of that current. The water likewise falls from the crest of the wave toward the bank (fig. 69, plate 13); but there, because the current is obstructed and delayed by the transverse motion of the same wave, it descends toward the bank, penetrating it with greater force, and by striking it <term>percotendola</term> <note>the act of the water hitting or "hammering" the bank</note>, creates an eddy.

->### CHAPTER XVII.<-

->*On the same.*<-

In every impact <term>percussione</term> <note>the forceful striking of water against a surface</note> of water against a narrowed bank or an obstacle in the bank, eddies are generated from the surface to the bottom. This is because, upon impact, the water rises up the height of the bank or obstacle, and gaining weight, it descends to the base. In the middle of this descent, it meets the water that had previously turned toward the bottom and is pushed back to the surface; there, overtaken by new arriving water and driven to the bottom in various swirls, it is carried along behind the main course of the water.

->### CHAPTER XVIII.<-

->*On the same.*<-

A bank that is set back to provide greater width to the canal will cause the immediate generation of an eddy. This is proven because the river, which acquires a sudden width, also acquires a sudden breadth of water, and the water that spreads out also decreases in depth;

<summary>Leonardo explains how eddies are formed by water striking obstacles or banks, describing a cycle where water rises upon impact, gains weight, and sinks to create vertical and horizontal rotations. He also notes that widening a channel creates immediate turbulence due to changes in water depth and breadth.</summary>

<keywords>hydraulics, eddies, fluid dynamics, river banks, wave mechanics, Leonardo da Vinci, water velocity</keywords>

->Del medesimo.<-

Delli due retrosi fatti dopo l' argine allargata, il primo è più potente. Come il retroso CBA (fig. 70. tav. 13.) per essere rinchiuso si getta fortemente verso il fondo, e per la quarantesimaterza di questo, che dice, che il retroso sarà più penetrabile, che avrà il labbro della sua bocca manco obliquo; questo l' avrà assai dritto ec.

## CAPITOLO XX.

->Del medesimo.<-

Se il canale acquisterà da ogni parte subita larghezza, esso genera retrosi per ogni parte, de' quali li primi saranno più potenti (fig. 71 tav. 13). Questa è manifesta per le due passate.

## CAPITOLO XXI.

->Del medesimo.<-

Se l' onda colonnale percuoterà li retrosi generati nell' uno degli argini allargati, allora tali retrosi rinchiusi si restringeranno, ed acquisteranno gran potenza. Questo accade, non solo perchè l' onda colonnale in tal caso alza l' acqua, ma anche perchè percotendo anch' essa nell' argine si moltiplica la forza, e li retrosi restano più dritti (fig. 72 tav. 13).

## CAPITOLO XXII.

->Del medesimo.<-

Se nell' uno degl' argini allargati sia posto alcuno obbietto sotto l' onda colonnale di tale obbietto, li retrosi che fiano generati saranno di gran potenza. Questo accade (fig. 73. tav. 14) perchè dove l' acqua per l' obbietto maggiormente si stringe l' onda generata più s' innalza, e per questo con maggior impeto discende verso l' argine, ed ivi si creano retrosi di maggior potenza ec.

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s analysis of water behavior when striking a river bank. It specifically explores what happens when a narrow channel suddenly widens or encounters an obstacle, creating complex circular currents.</meta>

LEONARDO DA VINCI 347

therefore, a sudden current is generated, which, throwing itself against the widened bank <term>argine</term> <note>the side or levee of a river or canal</note>, strikes it and divides into two eddies <term>retrosi</term> <note>circular or backward-flowing water patterns, such as whirlpools or eddies</note>.

## CHAPTER XIX.

->On the same.<-

Of the two eddies formed after the bank has widened, the first is the more powerful. Just as the eddy CBA (fig. 70. plate 13), by being enclosed, throws itself forcefully toward the bottom; and according to the forty-third [rule] of this treatise, which states that an eddy will have more penetrating force the less oblique the lip of its mouth is; this one will have it quite straight, etc. <note>Leonardo is referring back to a specific mathematical or physical proposition he established earlier in his notebook regarding the angle at which water enters a whirlpool.</note>

## CHAPTER XX.

->On the same.<-

If the channel should suddenly acquire width on every side, it generates eddies on every side, of which the first will be more powerful (fig. 71 plate 13). This is evident from the two previous chapters.

## CHAPTER XXI.

->On the same.<-

If the columnar wave <term>onda colonnale</term> <note>a wave that rises in a column-like shape, often where currents meet or hit an obstacle</note> strikes the eddies generated in one of the widened banks, then those enclosed eddies will become more constricted and will acquire great power <term>potenza</term> <note>the force, momentum, or kinetic energy of the water</note>. This happens not only because the columnar wave in such a case raises the water level, but also because by striking the bank itself, the force is multiplied, and the eddies remain more upright (fig. 72 plate 13).

## CHAPTER XXII.

->On the same.<-

If an object is placed in one of the widened banks beneath the columnar wave created by that object, the eddies that are generated will be of great power. This happens (fig. 73. plate 14) because where the water is most constricted by the object, the generated wave rises higher; for this reason, it descends toward the bank with greater impetus <term>impeto</term> <note>the momentum or surge of the water's movement</note>, and there eddies of greater power are created, etc.

<summary>Leonardo examines how sudden changes in a river's width or the presence of obstacles create powerful eddies, noting that the height of a wave directly increases the destructive force of the water against the bank.</summary>
<keywords>hydraulics, eddies, river banks, water power, fluid dynamics, wave height, obstacles</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s technical observations on hydraulic engineering and fluid dynamics, specifically focusing on how obstacles within a riverbed or along its banks alter the flow of water and create powerful erosive forces.</meta>

<warning>Text on the right edge of the page appears to be truncated or faded in this reproduction, leading to incomplete words at line endings.</warning>

LEONARDO DA VINCI 348

## CHAPTER XXIII.
### *On the same subject.*

Wherever an obstacle is placed in a widened bank <term>argine</term> <note>the side, levee, or embankment of a watercourse</note> following its columnar waves <term>onde colonnale</term> <note>vertical surges or column-like waves formed by converging currents</note>, the eddies <term>retrosi</term> <note>backward-flowing or circular currents, such as whirlpools or vortices</note> that strike the bank will be of greater power <term>potenza</term> <note>the force or kinetic energy of the water</note> than those that came before (fig. 74, plate 14). This is because the wave rises not only due to the narrowing of the channel, but also from the collision <unclear>of</unclear> one current with another; from this height, it descends toward the bank with greater impetus.

## CHAPTER XXIV.
### *On the same subject.*

If a side obstacle is placed that occupies a large part of the channel, not only will the aforementioned eddies strike its own bank, but eddies will also run from the surface to the bottom along the opposite bank. This happens because the water rises so high in the narrow mouth of the passage that, upon exiting, it does not only dash toward the bank—where the usual eddies are generated—but also falls to the bottom due to its own weight. There, in its rebound, it is oppressed by new falling water, and it revolves now below and now above, behind the path of the current.

## CHAPTER XXV.
### *On the same subject.*

If two equal side obstacles are placed, not only are lateral revolutions created at the banks after the water's discharge, but various circulations from the surface to the bottom also go revolving in the middle; this is manifest from the seventeenth [rule] and the previous one.

## CHAPTER XXVI.
### *On the eddies created by the impact of water against obstacles on the bottom underwater.*

If a rock <term>scoglio</term> <note>a submerged rock, reef, or large stone obstacle</note> that divides the flow of the water only in its lower parts is covered by the flowing water, the water passing over the top will fall behind it, landing at its base. The water that falls from such a depth swirls in a backward-spinning motion <note>original: "revertiginosamente"; Leonardo describes a complex, turbulent spiral that turns back against the main flow.</note> both below and above, because...

<summary>Leonardo explains how obstacles in a river channel—whether on the banks or submerged—create powerful eddies and vertical circulations that can erode the riverbed and embankments.</summary>
<keywords>hydraulics, eddies, river banks, water pressure, underwater obstacles, fluid dynamics, erosion, vortices</keywords>

<meta>The text is a reference work categorizing literary phrases and historical citations organized by specific characters and themes. This section focuses on various usages of the character for rank or official salary.</meta>

transforming the sea, they offer treasures as tribute; I employ you with praise and advance your rank to demonstrate the encouragement of loyalty and righteousness. Wang Rong, while in prison, composed a response to an interrogation stating: The respect shown to those of high and low rank is different. Zhu Zhicai's poem for the Seventh Night of the Seventh Month <note>the Qixi Festival</note> says: The Gourd and the Ox <note>constellations</note> carry the trays, how can the golden shuttle be thrown to the ground? It is utterly absurd.

### High Rank
History of Yuan, Annals of Emperor Yingzong: In the various districts and counties of the vast coastal regions, there are many vacant official posts. Those who are honest and willing to take these positions shall be advanced two grades in rank.

### Private Rank
Han Feizi: When Jisun was the minister of Lu, Zilu served as the magistrate of Hou. The state of Lu mobilized the masses in the fifth month to dig a long trench. During this task, Zilu used his own grain to make congee and rice to feed the laborers at the crossroads of Wufu.

### Combined Rank
Luxuriant Dew of the Spring and Autumn Annals: The method of examination is to match one's title and salary <note>original: "jue lu"</note> with their combined rank, calculate their days of service, and display their merits.

### Full Rank
Garden of Stories <note>original: "Shuo Yuan"</note>: Uncle Fan of Jin said: If the people have the appearance of hunger while the horses have the appearance of fullness, the ruler cannot maintain his position. Yan Yanzhi's Rhapsody on the Red and White Horse: They are placed in the depths of the Washing Dragon Pond and entrusted with the fodder of the Red Grain Storehouse.

### Supply Rank
Garden of Stories: Yanzi said: Now we speak of seeking out the elderly and weak who are not cared for, and the widowed and orphaned who are not recognized; these are discussed as having a lowly rank.

### Many Ranks
Discourses Weighed in the Balance <note>original: "Lunheng"</note>: King Cheng's talent was not equal to the Duke of Zhou; Duke Huan's wisdom was not equal to Guan Zhong. Yet Cheng and Huan received the mandate of honor, while Zhou and Guan received the mandate of rank. Zhang Jiuling's poem: In my later years, following many ranks, the fork in the road is truly not singular. Ouyang Xiu's poem: Diligent yet ashamed of clever officialdom, in poverty and lowliness I keep my many ranks.

### Gracious Rank
Xie Lingyun's poem: Having completed my term, how could I expect a gracious rank? Xie Zhuang's Memorial on Seeking Talent: Some are advanced in rank on the spot, others enter into the glory and favor of the court.

### Concurrent Rank
Xie Tiao's poem: Hurriedly going to serve at the Southern Peak, concurrently holding a rank with the name of the state.

### Retired Rank
Xie Tiao's poem: Resigning due to illness without waiting for the usual age, keeping one's retired rank. Emperor Yuan of Liang's Decree on Encouraging Farming: At the time when the Star Bird <note>a constellation marking spring</note> appears, it signals the year's prosperity in the spring; the Resting Dragon song is heard as the harvest is taken from the southern fields.

### Refined Rank
Jiang Hai's Petition on Taking the Proper Position: The path of the woodcutter follows the flourishing industry; great blessings and abundant prosperity are attained through refined rank.

### Pure and Clean
### Poor Rank
Xue Tinggui’s Imperial Decree appointing Wang Jian as the Acting Minister of War states: The Five Weapons <note>the five branches of the military</note> are in **Pure and Clean** order, bringing glory to the guest stairs <note>the ministerial ranks</note>.

### Official Rank
Han Yu’s poem says: After attaining **Official Rank**, he was placed among the thousand grades; his poetry and prose are equal to the Six Classics.

### Temple Rank
Meng Jiao’s poem says: Although the **Temple Rank** is not yet noble.

### Moving Rank
Bai Juyi’s Imperial Decree appointing Wang Bi as Acting Minister of the Ministry of Revenue and Regional Governor of Lingyan states: We promote you to the Earth Official <note>Ministry of Revenue</note> to honor your new commission, and reach the limit of **Moving Rank** to praise your past merits.

### Seniority Rank
Bai Juyi’s Imperial Decree appointing Zhang Jiatai as Vice Governor of Yanzhou states: The assistant to the military and prefecture commander holds a **Seniority Rank** that is not low. 

Liang Dao’s memorial states: Emperor Taizong deeply understood this intention; he first established the Chongwen Institute and built the Secret Pavilion to collect the books of the Four Treasuries. He selected the most famous literary talents in the empire to serve as collation officers. They were provided with current salaries and fed at the Great Palace, providing them with excellent **Seniority Rank**.

### Censorate Rank
Bai Juyi’s Imperial Decree appointing Cui Chuchen as Palace Censor states: To demonstrate favored renown, it is fitting to transfer you to the **Censorate Rank**.

### Formal Rank
Qian Xu’s Imperial Decree appointing Li Jiwen as Defense Commissioner of Longzhou states: Having employed a talented man, it is fitting that he receive a **Formal Rank**.

### Remaining Rank
Dai Shulun’s poem says: With graying hair at my temples, I resign from my **Remaining Rank**; the autumn wind enters my old home garden.

### Terrace Rank
Luo Yin’s poem says: The official grade is noble in the **Terrace Rank** <note>referring to the Censorate or high office</note>; the mountains and rivers are embraced by the Lucky Star.

### Sixth Rank
Yu Shao’s Record on the Wall of the Hanyuan County Magistrate’s Hall states: The state established this path through diligent worry; thus, we increase the **Sixth Rank** to encourage those with ability.

### Ritual Rank
Zhang Yuqing’s Rhapsody on Sacrificing to the Sovereign Earth states: The Field Master clears the wilds; the Minister of Rites performs the **Ritual Rank** duties.

### Flourishing Rank
Zheng Xie’s Decree for the Duke of Zheng State states: Maintaining the old position of the Left Chancellor, while also holding the **Flourishing Rank** of the Eastern Terrace.

### Comparable Rank
Sun Zhu’s Decree granting Consort Xing the title of Worthy Consort states: Since her **Comparable Rank** is that of the High Dukes, we must seek one who is virtuous and wise.

### Entrusted Rank
Su Zhe’s poem says: Ultimately I am fortunate for the lenient administration, which still allows me to keep my **Entrusted Rank**.

### Capital Rank
Ye Shi’s poem says: Before border merits could be reported, the Wise Sovereign felt regret; as the **Capital Rank** was about to be finalized, old friends felt sorrow.

pages.translation:
Had reached, and Latonia <note>the moon</note>, rejoicing in her snowy chariot, scattering her lights through the dark night, had dispersed the shadows, here the ether, conscious of the offspring, shone forth, the stars glittered in the highest heaven: when the angel, carried by winged feather from the ethereal stars, [arrived] into the green field: which a small band of shepherds was holding, and, taking care for their flock, they were alleviating the night watch with varied conversation. Approaching them, he addressed them with a friendly voice:
    Accept these things in your minds and turn your joyful faces, shepherds: I descend as a messenger from the higher hall: bringing to you the joyful words of salvation restored, for you and for all who eat of the earth with varied gifts, looking at heaven with raised light. Rejoice and seclude the sad cares from your mind: salvation is prepared for you, and an abundance of friendly first goods, you who look at heaven with raised light. The turning age has finally brought help to those wishing for it, and the arrival of GOD, because the greatest hero has proceeded to you today from the high-sounding Olympus. He who was immortal put on mortal limbs, he who was incorrupt chose to assume corrupt matter, so that he himself might repair the lost salvation. He to whom there is the greatest power in heaven, and to whom there is the highest power in the lands, deigned to be born into the world from a pure virgin and succeeded to the aerial airs of light. Rejoice therefore all, and exclude mourning from your mind, to whom the new offspring, the only hope of true salvation, has happened. If this promise had not come after a long time, the offspring born from an untouched virgin, all the races of men would be driven to the horrible kingdoms of Pluto and to the dense shadows by the judgment of GOD.

To this place, where they would suffer the punishment of crimes and of ancient evils for eternity: as the first parents deserved. Thus once the oracles of the ancient prophets taught, to whom God Almighty, ministering mind and tongue, added, and gave help to know the future beforehand: such things as the prophets did not sing with a false mouth. For when time had passed, Mary, about to give birth to the first offspring, although ignorant of a male chamber, went while pregnant to the ancestral shores in Bethlehem. The commands of Caesar, the sacred oracles of the gods, drove [them] here with their orders: where the virgin Mary gave birth to the offspring conceived from the holy spirit, and placed his tender limbs in a vile manger. I also teach you to hold the signs in a conceived mind. You will immediately see the divine limbs of the infant, in appearance similar to all sick mortals. He who made the sea, who made the lands, who made the thresholds of the upper heaven with God the father and the holy spirit: whom neither the orb of the earth, nor vast Olympus could contain, although countless [in power], a small manger contains him, and thin clothes of his own dress surround him.

Go therefore, swift ones, and proceeding to the holy city of David, receive the holiest divine powers of such a birth with pious vows, since the same one is the best King of men, Almighty, and he himself is the celestial Priest. Who, when he would destroy the horrible thresholds of Satan with divine weapons, and, Victor, would snatch into chains the Tartarean <note>infernal</note> princes, he recalled the human race, which had suffered many infernal things, from the blind shadows, and brought the saved one to the celestial stars. Let your entire goal of salvation stand in this boy, let a solid mind and faith rest fixed in him.

## PREFACE TO THE SECOND EDITION.

IT has been at the earnest wish of many students, members of the Theosophical Society, and of my Hermetic fratres of the Order of the <term>G.D.</term>, that I have made a revised translation of the “<term>Sepher Yetzirah</term>.” In this edition I have followed most closely the Hebrew version of Joannes Stephanus Rittangelius, which was printed in 1642 at Amsterdam, and I have forsaken many of the Latinised renderings which had been adopted in the First Edition, from the works of Postellus and Pistorius.

The Notes have been extended, and it is hoped that they explain and illustrate difficult passages, and render this abstruse treatise more comprehensible than it has been hitherto found.

W. W. W., F.T.S.

# SEPHER YETZIRAH.

---

## INTRODUCTION.

---

THE "Sepher Yetzirah," or "Book of Formation," is perhaps the oldest philosophical treatise which is yet extant in the Hebrew language. The great interest which has been evinced of late years in the Hebrew Kabalah, and the modes of thought and doctrine allied to it, has induced me to translate this volume from the original Hebrew texts, and to collate with them the Latin versions of mediæval authorities. Three important books of the "Zohar," or "Splendour," which is the great storehouse of Kabalistic teaching, have been for the first time translated into English by that skilful and erudite Kabalist, my fellow student in occult science, Mac Gregor Mathers, and the "Sepher Yetzirah" in an English translation is almost a necessary companion to these even more abstruse disquisitions: the two books indeed mutually explain each other.

The "Sepher Yetzirah" although this name means "The Book of Formation," is not in any sense a narrative of Creation, or a substitute Genesis, but it is a very ancient and instructive philosophical treatise upon one aspect of the origin of the universe and mankind; an aspect at once archaic and essentially Hebrew. The grouping of the processes of origin into an arrangement, at once alphabetic and numeral, is one only to be found in Semitic authors.

# THE BOOK OF FORMATION.

---

## INTRODUCTION.

---

The "Sepher Yetzirah," <note>original: "Sepher Yetzirah," meaning "Book of Formation"</note> or "Book of Formation," is perhaps the oldest philosophical treatise still in existence written in the Hebrew language. The great interest shown in recent years regarding the Hebrew Kabbalah <note>The Kabbalah is a traditional system of Jewish mysticism and self-knowledge</note> and its related schools of thought has led me to translate this volume from the original Hebrew texts, comparing them with the Latin versions produced by medieval scholars. Three important books of the "Zohar," or "Splendor"—which serves as the primary storehouse of Kabbalistic teaching—have been translated into English for the first time by the skillful and learned Kabbalist MacGregor Mathers, my fellow student in the occult sciences. This English translation of the "Sepher Yetzirah" is an almost essential companion to those even more difficult and complex discussions; indeed, the two books explain one another.

Although its name means "The Book of Formation," the "Sepher Yetzirah" is not a narrative of Creation in the sense of a replacement for the Book of Genesis. Instead, it is a very ancient and educational philosophical treatise on one specific perspective regarding the origin of the universe and humanity—a perspective that is both ancient and characteristically Hebrew. This method of organizing the processes of origin into a system that is simultaneously alphabetical and numerical is a feature found only among Semitic authors.

Attention must be called to the essential characteristic of Hebrew doctrines: the inseparable and necessary association—

These are his words: 'The sages of Babylon attacked Abraham on account of his faith; for they were all against him, although they were divided into three sects. The First thought that the Universe was subject to the control of two opposing forces, the one existing only to destroy the other; this is dualism. They held that there was nothing in common between the author of evil and the author of good. The Second sect admitted Three great Powers: two of them as in the first case, and a third Power whose function was to decide between...'"

<summary>This page explains the numerical and symbolic logic of the Kabbalah, distinguishing the Sepher Yetzirah's focus on the universe from the Zohar's focus on the divine nature. It also cites Rabbi Moses Botarel's claim that the patriarch Abraham authored the text to defend monotheism against Babylonian dualism.</summary>

had no idea of that. Perhaps after all you had better not let me see you.' After this I always covered my face on any occasion when he could possibly have seen me; but I noticed that he never looked my way, and it seemed clear that he had taken what I said about my own ugliness quite seriously.

One morning Shikibu no Omoto [one of the Empress's ladies] and I lay in the side-room (where we had slept that night) till the sun was well up. Suddenly we heard someone sliding back the door that leads into the main building, and there before us stood the Emperor and Empress! We were so much surprised that we simply lay helpless, while their Majesties stood by, laughing immoderately at our confusion. Presently they came across and stood half hidden behind the pile of rugs and cloaks (for we had buried ourselves head and all under our bedding), to watch the people going to and fro between the Palace and the guard-room. Several courtiers (not, of course, having the least idea who was inside the room) came to the window and saluted us. The Emperor was much amused and begged me not to give him away.

When their Majesties went back to the main building, the Empress said, ‘Come along, both of you,’ intending us to go on duty that minute. ‘Do at least give us time to make up our faces!’ I answered, and we stayed where we were. Later on, when Shikibu and I were still talking about their Majesties’ visit, we became conscious of something swarthy which had suddenly loomed up close to the front door of our room, and was visible through a chink in our curtains, where one flap had got caught up upon the framework. We thought it was only Noritaka,¹ but on looking more closely we saw that the face was not the least like his.

With a good deal of laughing and scuffling, we began pulling the curtain back into its place; but before we had finished doing so, we realized that it was Yukinari who had been looking at us. This was very annoying, for I had made a point of his never seeing me. Shikibu was sitting with her back to him, so she came out of it all right.
